title: Erdős Problem #525 — Minimum modulus of almost every sign polynomial
statement:
For each integer $n\geq 0$, let
$$
\mathcal P_n=\left\{P(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\varepsilon_k z^k:\ \varepsilon_k\in\{-1,1\}\right\},
$$
so that $|\mathcal P_n|=2^{n+1}$, and define
$$
m(P)=\min_{|z|=1}|P(z)|.
$$
As $n\to\infty$, is it true that
$$
\bigl|\{P\in\mathcal P_n:m(P)\geq 1\}\bigr|=o(2^n)?
$$
Equivalently, for a polynomial chosen uniformly from $\mathcal P_n$, does the probability that $|P(z)|<1$ for some $|z|=1$ tend to $1$? More generally, what is the typical size, or limiting distribution after suitable normalization, of $m(P)$? [Erdős (1961)](https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1961-22.pdf#page=33) [Erdős Problem #525](https://www.erdosproblems.com/525)

## Background

Erdős posed this question in 1961 in a discussion of random-sign polynomials and the Salem–Zygmund estimates for their maximum modulus. The minimum asks for a markedly different kind of information: whether the polynomial comes close to zero anywhere on the unit circle. With independent uniform signs, these are Kac polynomials with Rademacher coefficients. Littlewood later asked the stronger asymptotic question of whether the minimum tends to zero; that question led to estimates on its scale and, eventually, to a limiting-law problem. [Erdős (1961)](https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1961-22.pdf#page=33) [Universality of the minimum modulus for random trigonometric polynomials](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2101.07203) [Erdős Problem #525](https://www.erdosproblems.com/525)

## Known results

The first question and Littlewood’s stronger vanishing question were answered affirmatively: Kashin proved that the minimum tends to zero for almost all sign polynomials, and Konyagin sharpened the typical upper scale to $n^{-1/2+o(1)}$. In the complementary direction, Konyagin and Schlag showed that for every $\epsilon>0$ there is an absolute constant $C$ such that
$$
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\mathbb P\!\left(m(P_n)\leq \epsilon n^{-1/2}\right)\leq C\epsilon,
$$
where $P_n$ is uniformly chosen from $\mathcal P_n$. Thus the minimum is typically on the order of $n^{-1/2}$, rather than substantially smaller. [Erdős Problem #525](https://www.erdosproblems.com/525) [Universality of the minimum modulus for random trigonometric polynomials](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2101.07203)

Cook and Nguyen’s universality result identifies the limiting law for Rademacher coefficients. In the degree-$n$ normalization of the question, for an explicit constant $\lambda>0$ and every $\epsilon>0$,
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb P\!\left(m(P_n)>\epsilon n^{-1/2}\right)=e^{-\lambda\epsilon}.
$$
In particular, this gives a limiting distribution at the $n^{-1/2}$ scale and implies that the probability of $m(P_n)\geq 1$ tends to zero. The result is a universality theorem: the limiting behavior agrees with the Gaussian-coefficient model, although the coefficients need only satisfy the stated sub-Gaussian and variance hypotheses in the paper’s trigonometric-polynomial formulation.
